text: Course 2's reporting lessons taught you Reports, List views, and pivot tables. SLA reporting uses those exact same tools, pointed at a table most new administrators overlook: task_sla, not incident.

Every row in task_sla is one SLA instance attached to one record, carrying its own stage, a has_breached flag, and business_percentage — how much of the duration target has been consumed. An incident can have more than one task_sla row if more than one SLA applies to it.

The most common SLA report groups task_sla records where has_breached is true, by the Priority of the task or by assignment group. Breach rate by Priority tells you whether the target itself is realistic; breach rate by Assignment Group tells you whether it's a specific team's performance.

Confusing those two cuts is a common mistake — treating a high breach rate as automatically a staffing problem, or automatically an unrealistic target, when running both side by side usually reveals which one it actually is.

Breach count alone hides a lot. A team that resolves every ticket at 99% of target has a 0% breach rate, identical on a breach-count report to a team resolving at 40% of target with hours to spare. Averaging business_percentage tells you how close to the edge a team is really running.

A standard Report against task_sla answers how breach rate looks right now, or over a fixed date range — a snapshot. It can't show whether breach rate is improving, worsening, or cyclical, like worse on Mondays or at month-end.

Performance Analytics closes that gap, tracking task_sla breach rate as a real time series sampled on a schedule, with trend lines and target bands. Next up: the SLA Implementation Lab, building a full Priority 1 SLA end to end.
